claims.text: A sole trader is a business owned and controlled by one person, who takes the decisions, keeps the whole profit after tax and is personally responsible for every debt; a partnership is a business owned jointly by two or more partners who share the decisions, the profits and responsibility for debts.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A private limited company and a public limited company are both owned by shareholders and exist as separate legal entities whose shareholders enjoy limited liability; shares in a private limited company move with the founders' approval and are not offered to the general public, while a public limited company may sell shares to the general public on a stock exchange.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A franchise is an arrangement in which a franchisor sells the right to trade under its name and its proven business system to a franchisee, who pays a fee and usually a continuing share of sales and follows the franchisor's rules in return for an established brand and support.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A joint venture is a separate project or business formed when two or more businesses agree to work together on it, each contributing resources and sharing the risks and rewards of that one venture while staying independent.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An unincorporated business, such as a sole trader or a partnership, has no legal identity separate from its owners, so in law the owners and the business are the same person and the business's contracts, property and debts belong to its owners personally.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A limited company is an incorporated business: it exists in law as a separate legal entity that can own property, sign contracts, sue and be sued in its own name, and keep existing when its owners change.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Because a company is a separate legal person while an unincorporated business is not, ownership, risk and liability fall differently on the two groups: company shareholders risk the money they invested, while unincorporated owners can be made to pay business debts out of personal possessions.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Business risk is the chance that a business performs worse than its owners expect, so that some or all of the money they invested is lost, and owners of unincorporated forms may lose personal wealth beyond it as well.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Ownership means holding the business and controlling its decisions; it sits with one person in a sole trader, with the partners in a partnership, with the shareholders in a company, and with the state in a public corporation.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Limited liability means a shareholder's financial responsibility for a company's debts stops at the amount invested in the shares, so personal possessions are protected when the company cannot pay what it owes.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Unlimited liability means an owner is personally responsible for all of the business's debts, so creditors who are owed money can claim the owner's personal possessions; it applies to sole traders and partners.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A recommendation of a form of business organisation is justified by matching the features of each form - liability, capital, control, continuity and the cost and speed of formation - against the owners' situation and objectives.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The criteria usually conflict: incorporation brings limited liability and wider access to capital, but selling shares reduces the founder's share of profit and control, so the suitable form depends on which matters most in the given situation.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: For a growing unincorporated business, forming a private limited company tends to make large sums of share capital easier to raise and caps the owners' risk at what they invested, at the cost of sharing ownership, control and results with new shareholders.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A public corporation is a business organisation in the public sector that is owned by the state, set up by the government to provide an essential service, run by a board appointed by government, and financed by state funds as well as its own revenue.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Public corporations typically aim first at service coverage and controlled prices rather than profit, they often hold the sole right to supply an essential service, and their surpluses or losses belong to the state.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Governments set up public corporations where an essential service may not be profitable or reliable enough under private owners, because the state can absorb losses and direct investment toward national goals; the costs are that a public corporation can become inefficient without commercial pressure and its losses fall on taxpayers.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An entrepreneur and a sole trader are different kinds of idea: an entrepreneur is a person who starts a business and bears its risk, while a sole trader is one legal form of business organisation that an entrepreneur may choose, alongside a partnership, a company or a franchise.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.
